content: A bandicoot refers to any of approximately 20 species of small to medium-sized, terrestrial marsupial omnivores classified under the order Peramelemorphia. The term bandicoot is derived from the Telugu word pandi-kokku, which translates roughly to pig-rat and originally referred to the unrelated Indian Bandicoot Rat. Within the order Peramelemorphia, there are two other species groups known as bilbies. Historically, classification within this order was relatively straightforward, with two families being recognized: the short-legged, predominantly herbivorous bandicoots, and the longer-legged, more carnivorous bilbies. However, recent studies have revealed a more complex taxonomic structure. Initially, bandicoots inhabiting the rainforests of New Guinea and far northern Australia were identified as distinct from other bandicoots and were grouped into a separate family called Peroryctidae. More recently, taxonomists have reclassified these families, uniting them under the family Peramelidae. Within this family, the New Guinean species have been divided into four genera across two subfamilies, Peroryctinae and Echymiperinae, while the true bandicoots are categorized under the subfamily Peramelinae. An exception to this classification is the extinct Pig-footed Bandicoot, which has been assigned its own family, Chaeropodidae. A unique feature of bandicoot embryology is the development of a placenta-like organ that connects the embryo to the uterine wall, a characteristic not observed in other marsupials. This organ likely facilitates the transfer of nutrients from the mother to the developing embryo, although it is relatively small compared to the placental structures found in placental mammals.
